entries.577d7ebc3ff3b87791729caaa2723fd50e721da1: <div sID="gen12151" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="93" osisID="Ps.93" sID="Ps.93"/> <div eID="gen12151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12152" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12153" type="x-p"/> This short psalm sets forth the honour of the kingdom of God among men, to his glory, the terror of his enemies, and the comfort of all his loving subjects. It relates both to the kingdom of his providence, by which he upholds and governs the world, and especially to the kingdom of his grace, by which he secures the church, sanctifies and preserves it. The administration of both these kingdoms is put into the hands of the Messiah, and to him, doubtless, the prophet here hears witness, and to his kingdom, speaking of it as present, because sure; and because, as the eternal Word, even before his incarnation he was Lord of all. Concerning God's kingdom glorious things are here spoken. I. Have other kings their royal robes? So has he, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Have they their thrones? So has he, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.2">ver. 2</reference>. III. Have they their enemies whom they subdue and triumph over? So has he, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. IV. Is it their honour to be faithful and holy? So it is his, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.5">ver. 5</reference>. In singing this psalm we forget ourselves if we forget Christ, to whom the Father has given all power both in heaven and in earth.
entries.e51ecbbe8d2d8170fff4e31114188745b5a71634: <div eID="gen12153" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12152" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory and Majesty of God.</title> <div sID="gen12154" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is clothed with strength, <hi type="italic">wherewith</hi> he hath girded himself: the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thy throne <hi type="italic">is</hi> established of old: thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> from everlasting. <hi type="super">3</hi> The floods have lifted up, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves. <hi type="super">4</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> on high <hi type="italic">is</hi> mightier than the noise of many waters, <hi type="italic">yea, than</hi> the mighty waves of the sea. 5 Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , for ever. <div eID="gen12154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12155" type="x-p"/> Next to the being of God there is nothing that we are more concerned to believe and consider than God's dominion, that Jehovah is God, and that this God reigns (<reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">v. 1</reference>), not only that he is King of right, and is the owner and proprietor of all persons and things, but that he is King in fact, and does direct and dispose of all the creatures and all their actions according to the counsel of his own will. This is celebrated here, and in many other psalms: <hi type="italic">The Lord reigns.</hi> It is the song of the gospel church, of the glorified church (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">Rev. xix. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hallelujah; the Lord God omnipotent reigns.</hi> Here we are told how he reigns. <div eID="gen12155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12156" type="x-p"/> I. The Lord reigns gloriously: <hi type="italic">He is clothed with majesty.</hi> The majesty of earthly princes, compared with God's terrible majesty, is but like the glimmerings of a glow-worm compared with the brightness of the sun when he goes forth in his strength. Are the enemies of God's kingdom great and formidable? Yet let us not fear them, for God's majesty will eclipse theirs. <div eID="gen12156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12157" type="x-p"/> II. He reigns powerfully. He is not only clothed with majesty, as a prince in his court, but he is <hi type="italic">clothed with strength,</hi> as a general in the camp. He has wherewithal to support his greatness and to make it truly formidable. See him not only clad in robes, but clad in armour. Both <hi type="italic">strength and honour are his clothing.</hi> He can do every thing, and with him nothing is impossible. 1. With this power <hi type="italic">he has girded himself;</hi> it is not derived from any other, nor does the executing of it depend upon any other, but he has it of himself and with it does whatsoever he pleases. Let us not fear the power of man, which is borrowed and bounded, but fear him who has power to kill and cast into hell. 2. To this power it is owing that the world stands to this day. The world also is established; it was so at first, by the creating power of God, when he founded it upon the seas; it is so still, by that providence which upholds all things and is a continued creation; it is so established that though he has <hi type="italic">hanged the earth upon nothing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.7">Job xxvi. 7</reference>) yet <hi type="italic">it cannot be moved;</hi> all things <hi type="italic">continue to this day, according to his ordinance.</hi> Note, The preserving of the powers of nature and the course of nature is what the God of nature must have the glory of; and we who have the benefit thereof daily are very careless and ungrateful if we give him not the glory of it. Though God clothes himself with majesty, yet he condescends to take care of this lower world and to settle its affairs; and, if he established the world, much more will he establish his church, that it cannot be moved. <div eID="gen12157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12158" type="x-p"/> III. He reigns eternally (<reference osisRef="Ps.93.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy throne is established of old.</hi> 1. God's right to rule the world is founded in his making it; he that gave being to it, no doubt, may give law to it, and so his title to the government is incontestable: <hi type="italic">Thy throne is established;</hi> it is a title without a flaw in it. And it is ancient: it is <hi type="italic">established of old,</hi> from the beginning of time, before any other rule, principality, or power was erected, as it will continue when all other rule, principality, and power shall be put down, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>. 2. The whole administration of his government was settled in his eternal counsels before all worlds; for he does all according to the purpose which he purposed in himself; The chariots of Providence came down from between the mountains of brass, from those decrees which are fixed as the everlasting mountains (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.1">Zech. vi. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art from everlasting,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">thy throne is established of old;</hi> because God himself was from everlasting, his throne and all the determinations of it were so too; for in an eternal mind there could not but be eternal thoughts. <div eID="gen12158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12159" type="x-p"/> IV. He reigns triumphantly, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. We have here, 1. A threatening storm supposed: <hi type="italic">The floods have lifted up, O Lord!</hi> (to God himself the remonstrance is made) <hi type="italic">the floods have lifted up their voice,</hi> which speaks terror; nay, they have <hi type="italic">lifted up their waves,</hi> which speaks real danger. It alludes to a tempestuous sea, such as the wicked are compared to, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Isa. lvii. 20</reference>. The <hi type="italic">heathen rage</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>) and think to ruin the church, to overwhelm it like a deluge, to sink it like a ship at sea. The church is said to <hi type="italic">be tossed with tempests</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.11">Isa. liv. 11</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">floods of ungodly men</hi> make the saints <hi type="italic">afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Ps. xviii. 4</reference>. We may apply it to the tumults that are sometimes in our own bosoms, through prevailing passions and frights, which put the soul into disorder, and are ready to overthrow its graces and comforts; but, if the Lord reign there, even the winds and seas shall obey him. 2. An immovable anchor cast in this storm (<reference osisRef="Ps.93.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord himself is mightier.</hi> Let this keep our minds fixed, (1.) That God is on high, above them, which denotes his safety (they cannot reach him, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Ps. xxix. 10</reference>) and his sovereignty; they are ruled by him, they are overruled, and, wherein they rebel, overcome, <reference osisRef="Exod.18.11">Exod. xviii. 11</reference>. (2.) That he <hi type="italic">is mightier,</hi> does more <hi type="italic">wondrous things</hi> than <hi type="italic">the noise of many waters;</hi> they cannot disturb his rest or rule; they cannot defeat his designs and purposes. Observe, The power of the church's enemies is but <hi type="italic">as the noise of many waters;</hi> there is more of sound than substance in it. <hi type="italic">Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.46.17">Jer. xlvi. 17</reference>. The church's friends are commonly more frightened than hurt. God is mightier than this noise; he is mighty to preserve his people's interests from being ruined by these many waters and his people's spirits from being terrified by the noise of them. He can, when he pleases, command peace to the church (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.7">Ps. lxv. 7</reference>), peace in the soul, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa. xxvi. 3</reference>. Note, The unlimited sovereignty and irresistible power of the great Jehovah are very encouraging to the people of God, in reference to all the noises and hurries they meet with in this world, <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.2">Ps. xlvi. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen12159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12160" type="x-p"/> V. He reigns in truth and holiness, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.5">v. 5</reference>. 1. All his promises are inviolably faithful: <hi type="italic">Thy testimonies are very sure.</hi> As God is able to protect his church, so he is true to the promises he has made of its safety and victory. His word is passed, and all the saints may rely upon it. Whatever was foretold concerning the kingdom of the Messiah would certainly have its accomplishment in due time. Those testimonies upon which the faith and hope of the Old-Testament saints were built were very sure, and would not fail them. 2. All his people ought to be conscientiously pure: <hi type="italic">Holiness becomes thy house, O Lord! for ever.</hi> God's church is his house; it is a holy house, cleansed from sin, consecrated by God, and employed in his service. The holiness of it is its beauty (nothing better becomes the saints than conformity to God's image and an entire devotedness to his honour), and it is its strength and safety; it is the holiness of God's house that secures it against the many waters and their noise. Where there is purity there shall be peace. Fashions change, and that which is becoming at one time is not so at another; but holiness always becomes God's house and family, and those who belong to it; it is perpetually decent; and nothing so ill becomes the worshippers of the holy God as unholiness.  <chapter eID="Ps.93"/> <div eID="gen12160" type="x-p"/>

entries.6c364a230dd324d5d7c19d67645fc87fe42df6b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6590"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 93</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:1-5</reference>. This and the six following Psalms were applied by the Jews to the times of the Messiah. The theme is God's supremacy in creation and providence.</title> <div sID="gen10099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6590"/>1. God is described as a King entering on His reign, and, for robes of royalty, investing Himself with the glorious attributes of His nature. The result of His thus reigning is the durability of the world. <div eID="gen10099" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc75aa537a679d86ead7f33e58c2b6d65d088524: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6591"/><div sID="gen10100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6591"/>2-4. His underived power exceeds the most sublime exhibitions of the most powerful objects in nature (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.9">Psa 89:9</reference>). <div eID="gen10100" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f7130fb105fa104798c6b6be041ebeb7a0c72ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6592"/><div sID="gen10101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6592"/>5. While His power inspires dread, His revealed will should secure our confidence (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.19.7">Psa 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">25:10</reference>), and thus fear and love combined, producing all holy emotions, should distinguish the worship we offer in His house, both earthly and heavenly. <chapter eID="Ps.93"/>

entries.ea20370c1f33861d025ddba4f938d103e09e9cf9: <div eID="gen21707" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21708" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21709" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21709" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21708" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21710" type="x-p"/> The universal government of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.93.2">Psa 93:2</reference>; the opposition to that government, <reference osisRef="Psa.93.3">Psa 93:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.93.4">Psa 93:4</reference>; the truth of God's testimonies, <reference osisRef="Psa.93.5">Psa 93:5</reference>. <div eID="gen21710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21711" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title either in the Hebrew or Chaldee. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, state it to be "A song of praise of David for the day preceding the Sabbath, when the earth was founded;" but in such a title there is no information on which any man can rely. This Psalm is written as a part of the preceding in twelve of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. It was probably written at the close of the captivity by the Levites, descendants of Moses. <div eID="gen21711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21712" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21713" type="x-p"/> The Lord reigneth - He continues to govern every thing he has created; and he is every way qualified to govern all things, for he is clothed with majesty and with strength - dominion is his, and he has supreme power to exercise it; and he has so established the world that nothing can be driven out of order; all is ruled by him. Nature is his agent: or rather, nature is the sum of the laws of his government; the operations carried on by the Divine energy, and the effects resulting from those operations. <div eID="gen21713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21714" type="x-p"/> He hath girded himself - The girding with strength refers to the girding in order to strengthen the loins, arms, knees, etc. When a Hindoo is about to set off on a journey, to lift a burden, or to do something that requires exertion, he binds firmly his loose upper garment round his loins - Ward.
entries.b28e8eaeb83441a032e1c1d5ade34e483cbe448e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21715" type="x-p"/> Thy throne is established of old - There never was a time in which God did not reign, in which he was not a supreme and absolute Monarch; for he is from everlasting. There never was a time in which he was not; there never can be a period in which he shall cease to exist.
entries.bccdbf149557d2420c08bca1b411e7513bdd796e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21716" type="x-p"/> The floods have lifted up - Multitudes of people have confederated against thy people; and troop succeeds troop as the waves of the sea succeed each other.
entries.89d0687dd1bba7bc12684f470cdc15dbf10ddb4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21717" type="x-p"/> The Lord - is mightier than the noise of many waters - Greater in strength than all the peoples and nations that can rise up against him. <div eID="gen21717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21718" type="x-p"/> Mighty waves of the sea - Even the most powerful empires can prevail nothing against him; therefore those who trust in him have nothing to fear.
entries.3c03238fc3f54a1af750ff6446c89bc855159ef0: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21719" type="x-p"/> Thy testimonies are very sure - Thou wilt as surely fulfill thy word as thou wilt keep possession of thy throne. <div eID="gen21719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21720" type="x-p"/> Holiness becometh thine house - Thy nature is holy, all thy works are holy, and thy word is holy; therefore, thy house - thy Church should be holy. The building itself should be sanctified - should be so consecrated to thy worship alone, that it shall never be employed in any other service. The ministers of this Church should be holy, the members holy, the ordinances holy; its faith, its discipline, and its practice holy. And this at all times, and in all circumstances; for holiness becometh thine house-for ever," לארך ימים le-orech yamim, for length of days. During the whole lapse of time; till the sun and moon shall be no more. The old Psalter says the house of God is man's saule; and of this house holiness is נאוה naavah, "the ornament;" it produces that meek and quiet spirit which is in the sight of God of great price. No decoration of person nor simplicity of dress can supply the place of this heavenly clothing.  <chapter eID="Ps.93"/> <div eID="gen21720" type="x-p"/>

entries.ab12b82374e9504ca9e0891af597f5cb58dc00c8: <div eID="gen9921" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Royal Throne above the Sea of the Peoples</title> <div sID="gen9922" type="x-p"/> Side by side with those Psalms which behold in anticipation the Messianic future, whether it be prophetically or only typically, or typically and prophetically at the same time, as the kingship of Jahve’s Anointed which overcomes and blesses the world, there are others in which the perfected theocracy as such is beheld beforehand, not, however, as an appearing (<hi type="italic">parusia</hi>) of a human king, but as the appearing of Jahve Himself, as the kingdom of God manifest in all its glory. These theocratic Psalms form, together with the christocratic, two series of prophecy referring to the last time which run parallel with one another. The one has for its goal the Anointed of Jahve, who rules out of Zion over all peoples; the other, Jahve sitting above the cherubim, to whom the whole world does homage. The two series, it is true, converge in the Old Testament, but do not meet; it is the history that fulfils these types and prophecies which first of all makes clear that which flashes forth in the Old Testament only in certain climaxes of prophecy and of lyric too (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>), viz., that the parusia of the Anointed One and the parusia of Jahve is one and the same. <div eID="gen9922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9923" type="x-p"/> Theocracy is an expression coined by Josephus. In contrast with the monarchical, oligarchical, and democratic form of government of other nations, he calls the Mosaic form θεοκρατία, but he does so somewhat timidly, ὡς ἂν τις εἴποι βιασάμενος τὸν λόγον [c. <hi type="italic">Apion</hi>. ii. 17]. The coining of the expression is thankworthy; only one has to free one’s self from the false conception that the theocracy is a particular constitution. The alternating forms of government were only various modes of its adjustment. The theocracy itself is a reciprocal relationship between God and men, exalted above these intermediary forms, which had its first manifest beginning when Jahve became Israel’s King (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.15.18">Exo 15:18</reference>), and which will be finally perfected by its breaking through this national self-limitation when the King of Israel becomes King of the whole world, that is overcome both outwardly and spiritually. Hence the theocracy is an object of prediction and of hope. And the word מלך is used with reference to Jahve not merely of the first beginning of His imperial dominion, and of the manifestation of the same in facts in the most prominent points of the redemptive history, but also of the commencement of the imperial dominion in its perfected glory. We find the word used in this lofty sense, and in relation to the last time, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa 24:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa 52:7</reference>, and most unmistakeably in <reference osisRef="Rev.11.17">Rev 11:17</reference>; Psa 19:6. And in this sense יהוה מלך is the watchword of the theocratic Psalms. Thus it is used even in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.9">Psa 47:9</reference>; but the first of the Psalms beginning with this watchword is <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>-5. They are all post-exilic. The prominent point from which this eschatological perspective opens out is the time of the new-born freedom and of the newly restored state. <div eID="gen9923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9924" type="x-p"/> Hitzig pertinently says: “This Psalm is already contained <hi type="italic">in nuce</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.92.9">Psa 92:9</reference> of the preceding Psalm, which surely comes from the same author. This is at once manifest from the jerking start of the discourse in <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3">Psa 93:3</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.92.10">Psa 92:10</reference>), which resolves the thought into two members, of which the first subsides into the vocative יהוה.” The lxx (<hi type="italic">Codd. Vat.</hi> and <hi type="italic">Sin</hi>.) inscribes it: Εἰς τὴν ἡμέρην τοῦ προσαββάτου, ὅτε κατῴκισται ἡ γῆ, αἶνος ᾠδῆς τῷ Δαυίδ. The third part of this inscription is worthless. The first part (for which <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi> erroneously has: τοῦ σαββάτου) is corroborated by the Talmudic tradition. <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:1-5</reference> was really the Friday Psalm, and that, as is said in <hi type="italic">Rosh ha-shana</hi> 31 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, ומלך עליהן (בשׁשׁי) על שׁם שׁגמר מלאכתו, because God then (on the sixth day) had completed His creative work and began to reign over them (His creatures); and that ὅτε κατῴκισται (<hi type="italic">al</hi>. κατῴκιστο) is to be explained in accordance therewith: when the earth had been peopled (with creatures, and more especially with men).
entries.e5a42752aa8b82dd1230b6e3825d9224b59658e5: <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1-Ps.93.2">Psa 93:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9925" type="x-p"/> The sense of מלך (with <hi type="italic">ā</hi> beside <hi type="italic">Zinnor</hi> or <hi type="italic">Sarka</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.1">Psa 97:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.99.1">Psa 99:1</reference> beside <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>)<note placement="foot">It is well known that his pausal form of the <hi type="italic">3rd masc. praet</hi>. occurs in connection with <hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi>; but it is also found with <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Psa 112:10</reference> (the reading וכעס), <reference osisRef="Lev.6.2">Lev 6:2</reference> (גּזל), <reference osisRef="Josh.10.13">Jos 10:13</reference> (עמד), <reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">Lam 2:17</reference> (זמם; but not in <reference osisRef="Deut.19.19">Deu 19:19</reference>; Zec 1:6, which passages Kimchi counts up with them in his grammar <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi>); with <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.27">Isa 14:27</reference> (יעץ), Hos 6:1 (טרף), <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">Amo 3:8</reference> (שׁאג); with <hi type="italic">Teb|=r</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.5.18">Lev 5:18</reference> (שׁגג); and even with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.17">1Sa 7:17</reference> (שׁפט), and according to Abulwalîd with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> in 1Ki 11:2 (דּבק).)</note> is historical, and it stands in the middle between the present מלך ה and the future מלך :ה Jahve has entered upon the kingship and now reigns Jahve’s rule heretofore, since He has given up the use of His omnipotence, has been self-abasement and self-renunciation: how, however, He shows Himself in all His majesty, which rises aloft above everything; He has put this on like a garment; He is King, and now too shows Himself to the world in the royal robe. The first לבשׁ has <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>; then the accentuation takes לבשׁ ה together by means of <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, and עז התאזּר together by means of <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>. עז, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference>, points to the enemies; what is so named is God’s invincibly triumphant omnipotence. This He has put on (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>), with this He has girded Himself - a military word (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa 8:9</reference>): Jahve makes war against everything in antagonism to Himself, and casts it to the ground with the weapons of His wrathful judgments. We find a further and fuller description of this עז התאזר in <reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Isa 59:17</reference>; Isa 63:1., cf. Dan 7:9.<note placement="foot">These passages, together with <reference osisRef="Ps.93.1">Psa 93:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.1">Psa 104:1</reference>, are cited in <hi type="italic">Cant. Rabba</hi> 26 <hi type="italic">b</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic">Debarim Rabba</hi> 29 <hi type="italic">d</hi>), where it is said that the Holy One calls Israel כלה (bride) ten times in the Scriptures, and that Israel on the other hand ten times assigns kingly judicial robes to Him.</note> <div eID="gen9925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9926" type="x-p"/> That which cannot fail to take place in connection with the coming of this accession of Jahve to the kingdom is introduced with אף. The world, as being the place of the kingdom of Jahve, shall stand without tottering in opposition to all hostile powers (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Psa 96:10</reference>). Hitherto hostility towards God and its principal bulwark, the kingdom of the world, have disturbed the equilibrium and threatened all God-appointed relationships with dissolution; Jahve’s interposition, however, when He finally brings into effect all the abundant might of His royal government, will secure immoveableness to the shaken earth (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.75.4">Psa 75:4</reference>). His throne stands, exalted above all commotion, מאז; it reaches back into the most distant past. Jahve is מעולם; His being loses itself in the immemorial and the immeasurable. The throne and nature of Jahve are not incipient in time, and therefore too are not perishable; but as without beginning, so also they are endless, infinite in duration.
entries.e9844db4b16b3817af74dec90caecbb0d9373500: <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.5">Psa 93:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen9926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9927" type="x-p"/> All the raging of the world, therefore, will not be able to hinder the progress of the kingdom of God and its final breaking through to the glory of victory. The sea with its mighty mass of waters, with the constant unrest of its waves, with its ceaseless pressing against the solid land and foaming against the rocks, is an emblem of the Gentile world alienated from and at enmity with God; and the rivers (floods) are emblems of worldly kingdoms, as the Nile of the Egyptian (Jer 44:7.), the Euphrates of the Assyrian (Isa 8:7.), or more exactly, the Tigris, swift as an arrow, of the Assyrian, and the tortuous Euphrates of the Babylonian empire (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>). These rivers, as the poet says whilst he raises a plaintive but comforted look upwards to Jahve, have lifted up, have lifted up their murmur, the rivers lift up their roaring. The thought is unfolded in a so-called “parallelism with reservation.” The perfects affirm what has taken place, the future that which even now as yet is taking place. The ἅπαξ λεγ. דּכי signifies a striking against (<hi type="italic">collisio</hi>), and a noise, a din. One now in <reference osisRef="Ps.93.4">Psa 93:4</reference> looks for the thought that Jahve is exalted above this roaring of the waves. מן will therefore be the <hi type="italic">min</hi> of comparison, not of the cause: “by reason of the roar of great waters are the breakers of the sea glorious” (Starck, Geier), - which, to say nothing more, is a tautological sentence. But if מן is comparative, then it is impossible to get on with the accentuation of אדירים, whether it be with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> (Ben-Asher) or <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> (Ben-Naphtali). For to render: More than the roar of great waters are the breakers of the sea glorious (Mendelssohn), is impracticable, since מים רבים are nothing less than ים (Isa 17:12.), and we are prohibited from taking אדירים משׁברי־ים as a parenthesis (Köster), by the fact that it is just this clause that is exceeded by אדיר במרום ה. Consequently אדירים has to be looked upon as a second attributive to מים brought in afterwards, and משׁבּרי־ים (the waves of the sea breaking upon the rocks, or even only breaking upon one another) as a more minute designation of these great and magnificent waters (אדירים, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.15.10">Exo 15:10</reference>),<note placement="foot">A Talmudic enigmatical utterance of R. Azaria runs: באדירים יבא אדיר ויפרע לאדירים מאדירים, Let the glorious One (Jahve, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.4">Psa 93:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Isa 10:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa 33:21</reference>) come and maintain the right of the glorious ones (Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference>) against the glorious ones (the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.10">Exo 15:10</reference> according to the construction of the Talmud) in the glorious ones (the waves of the sea, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.4">Psa 93:4</reference>).)</note>, and it should have been accented: מים רבים אדירים משברי ים | מקלות. Jahve’s celestial majesty towers far above all the noisy majesties here below, whose waves, though lashed never so high, can still never reach His throne. He is King of His people, Lord of His church, which preserves His revelation and worships in His temple. This revelation, by virtue of His unapproachable, all-overpowering kingship, is inviolable; His testimonies, which minister to the establishment of His kingdom and promise its future manifestation in glory, are λόγοι πιστοί καὶ ἀληθινοί, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">Rev 19:9</reference>; Rev 22:6. And holiness becometh His temple (נאוה־קדשׁ, <hi type="italic">3rd praet. Pilel</hi>, or according to the better attested reading of Heidenheim and Baer, נאוה;<note placement="foot">The Masora on Ps 147 reckons four נאוה, one ונאוה, and one נאוה eno d, and therefore our נאוה is one of the יז מלין דמפקין אלף וכל חד לית מפיק (cf. Frensdorf’s <hi type="italic">Ochla we-Ochla</hi>, p. 123), i.e., one of the seventeen words whose <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> is audible, whilst it is otherwise always quiescent; e.g., כּמוצאת, otherwise מוצאת.</note> therefore the feminine of the adjective with a more loosened syllable next to the tone, like יחשׁב־לּי in Ps 40:18), that is to say, it is inviolable (sacrosanct), and when it is profaned, shall ever be vindicated again in its holiness. This clause, formulated after the manner of a prayer, is at the same time a petition that Jahve in all time to come would be pleased to thoroughly secure the place where His honour dwells here below against profanation.  <chapter eID="Ps.93"/> <div eID="gen9927" type="x-p"/>

entries.d11d8f939982d400085c4aead6a38024ab0e20ff:
PSALM 93
The psalm commences with the celebration of the infinite glory of God. It is then declared that such is his faithfulness that he never deceives his own people, who, embracing his promises, wait with tranquil minds for their salvation amidst all the tempests and agitations of the world.
Psalm 93:1-2
1. Jehovah hath reigned, he hath clothed himself with majesty:
Horsley translates, —
“Jehovah is King, Jehovah is gorgeously arrayed.”
And, on the second line, he has the following note: — “The construction of the original is doubtful, though the sense be obvious. The text may be expounded in either of these two ways; יהוה (Jehovah) לבש (hath put on) גאות לבש (majesty of dress;) or, גאות לבש (majesty of dress) [is] לבש (the dress) יהוה (of Jehovah.)”
Jehovah hath clothed himself with strength, he hath girded himself:
See volume 2, page 455, note 2. Bishop Lowth supposes that here, as well as in that passage, there is an allusion to the precious and magnificent ornaments of the priests’ attire. “Such,” says he, “was the gracefulness, such the magnificence of the sacerdotal vestments, especially those of the High Priest; so adapted were they, as Moses says, (Exodus 28:2,) to the expression of glory and beauty, that to those who were impressed with an equal opinion of the sanctity of the wearer, nothing could possibly appear more venerable and sublime. To these, therefore, we find frequent allusions in the Hebrew poets, when they have occasion to describe extraordinary beauty or comeliness, or to delineate the perfect form of supreme Majesty. The elegant Isaiah (Isaiah 61:10) has a most beautiful idea of this kind when he describes, in his own peculiar manner, (that is, most magnificently,) the exultation and glory of the Church, after its triumphal restoration. Pursuing the allusion, he decorates her with the vestments of salvation, and clothes her in a robe of righteousness. He afterwards compares the Church to a bridegroom dressed for the marriage, to which comparison incredible dignity is added by the word Ikohen, a metaphor plainly taken from the apparel of the priests, the force of which, therefore, no modern language can express. No imagery, indeed, which the Hebrew writers could employ, was equally adapted with this to the display (as far as the human powers can conceive or depict the subject) of the infinite majesty of God, ‘Jehovah’ is therefore introduced by the Psalmist as ‘clothed with glory and with strength,’ (Psalm 93:1,) he is ‘girded with power,’ (Psalm 65:7;) which are the very terms appropriated to the describing of the dress and ornaments of the priests.” — Lectures on the Sacred Poetry of the Hebrews, volume 1, pages 174, 175.
he hath also established the world, it shall not be moved. 2. Thy throne is stable;
“Ou, prepare.” — Fr. marg. “Or, prepared.”
from then, from everlasting art thou.
 
1 Jehovah hath reigned We here see what I have lately adverted to, that in the power of God there is exhibited to us matter of confidence; for our not investing God with the power which belongs to him, as we ought to do, and thus wickedly despoiling him of his authority, is the source of that fear and trembling which we very often experience. This, it is true, we dare not do openly, but were we well persuaded of his invincible power, that would be to us an invincible support against all the assaults of temptation. All admit in word what the prophet here teaches, That God reigns; but how few are there who oppose this shield to the hostile powers of the world, as it becomes them to do, that they may fear nothing however terrible? In this then consists the glory of God, that he governs mankind according to his will. It is said that he clothes himself with majesty and strength; not that we ought to imagine that there is any thing in him which is derived from another, but it is intended by the effect and indubitable experience to show his wisdom and righteousness in the government of mankind. The Psalmist proves that God will not neglect or abandon the world, from the fact that he created it. A simple survey of the world should of itself suffice to attest a Divine Providence. The heavens revolve daily, and, immense as is their fabric, and inconceivable the rapidity of their revolutions, we experience no concussion — no disturbance in the harmony of their motion. The sun, though varying its course every diurnal revolution, returns annually to the same point. The planets, in all their wanderings, maintain their respective positions. How could the earth hang suspended in the air were it not upheld by God’s hand? By what means could it maintain itself unmoved, while the heavens above are in constant rapid motion, did not its Divine Maker fix and establish it? Accordingly the particle אף, aph, denoting emphasis, is introduced — Yea, he hath established it.

entries.15d0a3455b8b6de5192f2d697a79b0934a122541:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="93" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. XCIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm contains an assertion or declaration of Gods sove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raign and universal dominion in and over the whole world. Which is here set forth partly for the comfort of Gods Church and People against all the assaults of their numerous and potent Adversaries; and partly to give an intimation and assurance of the accomplishment of that great Promise of the Kingdom of the Messias, which was not to be con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fined to the Israelites, but to be extended to all the Nati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons of the Earth: which, though wonderful in our Eyes, the Supream and Almighty Ruler of the World could<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> easily effect. This and the six following Psalms, according to the opinion of the Hebrew Doctors, belong to the times of the Messias.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 96. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> & 97. 1. & 9<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 1.</ns0:note> THE LORD reigneth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He is the King and Governour not onely of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> but of the whole World, as the last clause of the Verse expounds it: and accordingly he will in his due time set up his Empire over all Nations in the hands of his Son the Messias.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 104. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> he is clo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thed with majesty, the LORD is clothed with strength <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That Majesty and strength which he always had in himself, he now hath and will shortly much more shew it forth in the Eyes of all people.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>wherewith</ns0:hi> he hath girded himself: the world also is established, that it cannot be moved <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The effect of Gods Government of the World shall be this, that he will order and over-rule all the Confusi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons, and Divisions, and Hostilities in the World, so as they shall end in an orderly, peaceable and happy settlement, and in the erection of that Kingdom of the Messias which can ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver be moved.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 45. 6.</ns0:note> Thy throne is established <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from then.</ns0:note> of old: thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> from everlasting. <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And this Kingdom of thine is no new or up start King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, as it may seem to the ignorant World, but the most antient of all Kingdoms, being from Everlasting to Everlast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, although it was not always equally manifested in the World.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 The flouds <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Enemies of thy Kingdom, who are oft compared to Flouds for their numbers, force, rage, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 8. 7, 8. and 17. 12, 13. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 46. 7, 8.</ns0:note> have lifted up, O LORD, the flouds have lifted up their voice: the flouds lift up their waves <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Have both by their words and actions made opposition against it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 The LORD on high <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> mightier than the noise of many waters, <ns0:hi>yea, than</ns0:hi> the mighty waves of the sea <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The King of Heaven is too strong for all Earthly Poten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tates and will subdue them under his feet.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Thy testimonies <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thy words: either 1. thy Precepts, which are commonly called Gods <ns0:hi>testimonies.</ns0:hi> And so having spoken of Gods Kingdom, he now sheweth that the Laws of that King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom are just, and true, and holy; which is a singular com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mendation of it. Or, 2. thy Promises, as may be gathered from the following words, <ns0:hi>are sure,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>true,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>faithful;</ns0:hi> which attribute properly belongs, and every where in Scripture is ascribed to Promises rather than to Precepts. And the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises no less than the Precepts are Gods <ns0:hi>Testimonies,</ns0:hi> or the Witnesses or Declarations of his mind and will to Mankind. And he seems here to speak of those great and precious Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises concerning the erection and establishment of his King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom in the World by the Messias. Which, faith he, are in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fallibly true and shall certainly be accomplished in thy time.</ns0:note> are very sure: holiness becometh thine house <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This is to be understood, either 1. of Gods Church or People, who are sometimes called Gods <ns0:hi>House,</ns0:hi> and whose business and delight is in Gods House and service there per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formed. So the sence is, It becometh thy people to be holy in all their approaches to thee, and worshippings of thee. Or rather 2. of God himself, who dwelt in his House, from whence he gave forth his Oracles, and where all his testimo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nies were kept upon record. This seems better to suit with the context, the business of this Psalm being rather to describe the Dominion of God than the duty of his people. And so the sence seems to be this, Holiness is the constant Ornament and glory of thy House. Or, it becometh thee who dwellest in thy House to be holy in all thy words and actions; and therefore thy testimonies are very sure, and thou wilt un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doubtedly fulfil all thy Promises. For <ns0:hi>holiness</ns0:hi> seems to be here taken for Gods faithfulness, as it is <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 60. 6. and 89. 35. <ns0:hi>or,</ns0:hi> which comes to the same thing, for his justice or righteousness, whereby he is obliged to make good all his promises, as that word is very commonly used.</ns0:note>, O LORD, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of days.</ns0:note> for ever.</ns0:p>
